The Krebs cycle is also called the citric acid cycle and occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.

Each Krebs cycle turn produces 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP; two turns per glucose produce 4 CO2, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 2 ATP.
The electron transport chain occurs along the inner mitochondrial membrane; NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons, proton pumping creates a gradient, and ATP synthase uses returning protons to make ATP.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water.
The electron transport chain produces about 28 to 34 ATP per glucose.
NADH yields more ATP than FADH2 because its electrons enter the chain earlier.
Older textbooks often give 36 to 38 ATP per glucose, while newer ones give about 30 to 32 ATP.
